tier_rationale: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are real (confirmed by FCC grant 2ACZS-R05010, DTS/Bluetooth-band module, matching the model number 'R05010' printed on the manual's title page and packing-list page), but the manufacturer's own operating manual documents no Ricoh-operated cloud service for this camera at all. The full 'Sharing Images' chapter covers exactly two paths: USB transfer to a computer, and Bluetooth/Wi-Fi pairing to Ricoh's 'Image Sync' companion app, which pairs directly to the camera's own radio (camera generates its own SSID/password; the app connects to that) with no sign-in step described anywhere in the pairing procedure. A full-text search of the manual for 'cloud', 'account', 'sign-in' and 'login' returns nothing tied to camera operation — the only web step in the entire manual is a one-time, explicitly optional customer-support registration page for firmware-update emails. No vendor cloud endpoint exists to name, which is the D1 test: radio and app present, no cloud to be optional about.
the_unplug_test: Nothing changes. Getting Started in Ricoh's own manual is battery, SD card, power on, set language and date, format the card, shoot — no app step, no activation, no account, at any point. Turn the camera's Wi-Fi and Bluetooth off entirely (both ship off by default and must be manually enabled) and you lose exactly one thing: pushing images to a phone through the Image Sync app for wireless transfer or remote control. There is no Ricoh cloud behind any of this to lose — the manual documents no cloud service for the camera at all, unlike Fujifilm's Timeline or GoPro's Cloud subscription.
offline_losses: wireless image transfer to a phone via the Image Sync app (Bluetooth/Wi-Fi)
remote camera operation from the Image Sync app

sources.supports: Manufacturer's own RICOH GR IIIx Operating Manual (filed as the FCC user-manual exhibit for grant 2ACZS-R05010, model R05010, matching the camera's printed model code). Getting Started (pp.37-46) covers only battery/SD-card insertion, power-on, language/date, and card formatting — no app, account, or activation step. 'Sharing Images' (pp.110-116) documents only USB-to-computer transfer and direct Bluetooth/Wi-Fi pairing to the 'Image Sync' app with no sign-in step in the pairing procedure. A full-text search of the extracted manual for 'cloud', 'account', 'sign-in' and 'login' found no camera-operation step gated behind any of them; the only web step in the manual is an optional customer-support registration for firmware-update emails (p.2).

FCC grant summary for grantee RICOH IMAGING COMPANY, LTD. (grantee code 2ACZS): model R05010, digital camera, 2402-2480 MHz Bluetooth/Wi-Fi band radio module, confirming the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios present in the device and that Ricoh files real equipment grants for its camera line (sibling-control context: grantee also holds R02010, R03010 and R09010 digital-camera grants).

open_questions: Whether the GR IIIx remains a current, in-production SKU as of this record's date, or has been superseded in Ricoh's lineup by a newer GR-series model, was not confirmed — Ricoh's own product pages could not be fetched (returned 404 on every guessed URL), so availability is left unknown rather than guessed.
Current US price could not be confirmed from a fetchable manufacturer or retailer page within budget.
Whether firmware updates can be declined, and what telemetry (if any) the camera or Image Sync app sends to Ricoh, are unconfirmed.

Whether Ricoh operates any cloud service for other camera lines (e.g. a newer GR model or the Pentax DSLR line) that might later apply to a GR IIIx firmware update was not checked — nothing in the current manual suggests one exists for this model.
notes: A clean control case for the D1/D2 boundary this project cares about: unlike the Fujifilm X100VI (D2, because Fujifilm operates a real 'network service' cloud behind its Timeline feature) and the GoPro HERO13 Black (D2, because GoPro Cloud is a real paid backend), Ricoh's GR IIIx manual describes no cloud endpoint anywhere — the Image Sync app is peer-to-peer only. That absence, not just the radios, is what keeps this at D1 rather than D2.
